review.alternative: Athletes who already experience lower self-regulation might independently seek out AI recommendations rather than AI usage causing the outsourcing.
review.would_change_mind: Longitudinal panel data showing that baseline self-regulation levels do not predict subsequent AI adoption.

claims.statement: AI training recommendation dependence is positively associated with body signal outsourcing and a reduced sense of self-regulation among athletes.

support.explanation: The source demonstrates the initial links in the serial association model between AI dependence and reduced self-regulation via body signal outsourcing.
support.passage: AI training recommendation dependence was significantly and positively associated with body signal outsourcing tendency, which was, in turn, positively associated with a reduced sense of self-regulation.

actions.findings: AI training recommendation dependence is positively associated with body signal outsourcing and a reduced sense of self-regulation among athletes. [source-d9addfec171d4b5d]
actions.limitations: The findings are based on cross-sectional questionnaire data from 381 athletes, which limits causal inference and requires longitudinal validation.
actions.next_questions: How do these serial association pathways vary across different types of skill-dominant versus physical-dominant sports over extended training cycles?
actions.reason: Revising notebook findings with new empirical sources detailing AI dependency pathways in athletes.
